public.title: Design a Reliable Toast Notification Layer
public.prompt: A product team needs non-blocking status messages that any screen can trigger. Design the frontend boundaries for displaying, dismissing, and announcing several messages without leaving timers behind.

clarifications.prompt: Which parts of the application need to create a toast?
Can a toast contain an action that the user may need to complete?
Which messages may disappear automatically and which must remain?
How many messages can arrive during a short burst?
How urgent are these messages for assistive technology?
Should messages survive client-side route changes?

requirements.description: Permitted timers preserve remaining time through relevant user interaction and page visibility changes.

requirements.title: Accessible status delivery
requirements.description: Announcements are restrained and controls remain keyboard reachable without stealing focus.

requirements.title: Complete lifecycle cleanup
requirements.description: Dismissal, teardown, and replacement release every owned timer and listener.

public.title: Design a Race-Safe Autocomplete

Should query state survive route navigation or page reload?

public.title: Design a Resilient AI Chat Composer
public.prompt: Design the frontend boundaries for an AI chat composer with composition-safe input, recoverable drafts, attachment readiness, one logical send, and a streamed assistant response. Stop, retry, and navigation must not let stale events corrupt a newer turn.

clarifications.prompt: How is an unsent draft scoped, persisted, and restored across navigation or reload?
Which IME, Enter-key, autosize, and focus behaviors must the composer preserve?
Which attachment phases block sending, and how can failed items recover?
Can the server accept a send when its transport response is lost or retried?
Can stream events arrive late, repeat, or belong to a turn that is no longer visible?
Does closing local transport prove that generation stopped on the server?

requirements.title: Accessible recovery controls

clarificationAnswers.answer: Unsent text must survive navigation or reload, remain isolated between accounts and conversations, and not disappear while a send has an uncertain outcome.
IME users must finish composition without accidental submission. Text-area growth stays bounded, and keyboard and focus behavior remains usable after send, Stop, attachment removal, or failure.
An attachment may still be local, transferring, ready, or failed when Send is pressed. Incomplete items cannot be sent, and one failure must not discard recoverable text or other attachments.
Yes. The server may accept a request even when the client receives no response. Repeating the user's single send must not create a duplicate logical message.
Yes. Events may arrive late or more than once, including after the user opens another conversation. Applying one twice or rendering it in the wrong conversation is invalid.
No. The local connection can close while generation is still running, and a Stop response can be lost. The UI must not report an unconfirmed terminal outcome.

responseActions.label: Clear the old partial response
responseActions.description: Remove the visible partial response when navigation selects another conversation.

responseActions.label: Retry Stop under a new command

clarificationAnswers.answer: A dashboard normally contains twenty to fifty charts or tables. Their data loads independently, and several visualizations are costly to rerender.
Desktop and tablet permit spatial editing. A phone needs a readable single-column order and a non-spatial reorder path; pixel-perfect parity is unnecessary.
Overlap is prohibited. The outcome must be predictable and reversible; either displacement or a blocked placement is acceptable if the interface explains it.
The layout follows the signed-in user across devices. Saving begins after a completed move, resize, reset, or undo, while editing remains available during the request.
Yes. Another tab can publish a newer revision. The service detects a stale precondition and returns the latest document rather than accepting a silent overwrite.
A keyboard user can move or resize by grid steps, retain focus on the tile, hear concise position and size updates, and use a list-style fallback.

responseActions.label: Swap the preview to revision 13
responseActions.description: Replace the active geometry as soon as the newer document arrives.

responseActions.label: Resubmit revision 12 as authoritative
responseActions.description: Send the local snapshot again with precedence over the returned document.

Widget-owned interaction and pointer-only pixel geometry fragment collision rules and exclude equivalent editing paths.

public.title: Design a Burst-Safe Live Chart

clarificationAnswers.answer: The chart shows up to four series. Each normally emits about two samples per second, with an occasional burst of one hundred accepted samples. It must remain usable for hours on desktop and mid-range mobile devices.
The live client keeps a five-minute window. Users may pause and inspect that window; older history is an abstract server query outside this design.

Each envelope has series identity, timestamp, stable sample identity, and an optional monotonic per-series sequence. Duplicates and gaps can occur; the source supports a cursor repair window or authoritative recent snapshot.

Exact bounded recent retention or an explicitly configured aggregate-window policy is acceptable. Visual commit cadence never decides which accepted samples survive, and gaps are never synthesized away.
Animation frames may pause while hidden, transport may continue or reconnect, and the container may resize before the tab returns. No renderer primitive or worker is mandatory without measurement.

The chart exposes its name, units, current values, range or trend, and freshness through a keyboard-usable semantic inspector. Reduced motion is respected and live regions summarize state changes instead of announcing every sample.

responseActions.label: Mark the next sample live
